resident.chief_complaint: Progressive difficulty walking, declining balance, and neuropathic pain in the extremities for one year.
resident.history: A 63-year-old male presented with a one-year history of progressive difficulty walking, declining balance, and neuropathic pain in his extremities. He was graded Nurick grade 3 and modified Japanese Orthopaedic Association (mJOA) score of 15. Cervical MRI showed severe cervical stenosis from C2-C3 to C5-C6 with associated hyperintense intramedullary signal change at C5-C6.
resident.physical_exam: Temperature 36°C, blood pressure 189/96 mmHg, heart rate 54 bpm. Physical examination notable for decreased cervical range of motion because of pain. The patient exhibited 5/5 strength in all muscle groups of the upper and lower extremities except for 4/5 strength in bilateral biceps and triceps. Sensation to light touch was decreased in bilateral upper and lower extremities. Bilateral upper and lower extremities revealed hyperreflexia.
key_positive_signs: 4/5 strength in bilateral biceps and triceps
Decreased sensation to light touch in bilateral upper and lower extremities
Bilateral upper and lower extremity hyperreflexia
Decreased cervical range of motion due to pain
resident.past_history: 15 pack-year smoking history, poorly controlled hypertension, medications metoprolol tartrate 25 mg twice daily and oxycodone 20 mg twice daily, remote lumbar transforaminal interbody fusion in 2001.
resident.public_message: This is a 63-year-old male with a one-year history of progressive difficulty walking, declining balance, and neuropathic extremity pain (Nurick grade 3, mJOA 15). Cervical MRI demonstrated severe stenosis from C2-C3 to C5-C6 with T2 hyperintense signal change at C5-C6. Past medical history includes a 15 pack-year smoking history, poorly controlled hypertension, medications metoprolol tartrate 25 mg BID and oxycodone 20 mg BID, and remote lumbar transforaminal interbody fusion in 2001. Vital signs: temperature 36°C, blood pressure 189/96 mmHg, heart rate 54 bpm. Physical exam showed decreased cervical range of motion due to pain, 4/5 strength in bilateral biceps and triceps (otherwise 5/5), decreased light touch sensation bilaterally, and bilateral hyperreflexia. Hemoglobin 15 g/dL.

imaging.public_message: Reporting the case record's description of the imaging; the films were not available for review. The record describes severe cervical stenosis from C2-3 through C5-6, with associated hyperintense intramedullary cord signal change at C5-6. The direction of compression is not stated. These findings correlate highly with the reported progressive myelopathic symptoms.

neurology.localization: Cervical myelopathy, with the lesion most consistent with the cervical spinal cord at C5-C6 given the intramedullary signal change and bilateral upper extremity weakness plus hyperreflexia; the hyperreflexia in all four limbs localizes to the upper motor neuron pathways above C5.

red_flags.finding: Remote lumbar transforaminal interbody fusion (2001) with reported lower extremity symptoms.
red_flags.rationale: Does not explain the upper extremity hyperreflexia or weakness, and the lower extremity upper motor neuron signs are readily attributed to the cervical lesion; no evidence of active lumbar pathology is provided, so it does not change the indication or plan.

red_flags.finding: Neuropathic pain in all extremities and symmetric decreased light touch sensation, without a documented sensory level or peripheral nerve examination.
red_flags.rationale: These features could suggest a coexisting peripheral neuropathy or central sensitization, but the presence of hyperreflexia and upper motor neuron signs indicates that cervical cord compression is the dominant cause of the myelopathic syndrome. This does not change the indication for addressing the cervical stenosis, though further electrodiagnostic testing could be considered if symptoms persist or confound assessment.

neurology.public_message: The examination localizes to the cervical spinal cord: bilateral upper and lower extremity hyperreflexia, bilateral biceps/triceps weakness, and gait difficulty are consistent with a cervical myelopathy, and the MRI findings of severe stenosis from C2-C3 to C5-C6 with cord signal change at C5-C6 explain the dominant syndrome (match level high). Two coexisting findings are noted: (1) the remote lumbar fusion does not alter the cervical localization or plan, and (2) the neuropathic pain and symmetric sensory loss raise the possibility of a coexisting peripheral neuropathy or central sensitization, but they do not change the indication for addressing the cervical stenosis because hyperreflexia indicates central nervous system involvement.

anesthesia.public_message: ASA grade III. Intraoperative mean arterial pressure target 85 mmHg. Blood loss risk: moderate. Extubation difficulty: unassessable because no formal airway assessment is recorded. Prone position tolerance: moderate.

physiatrist_opening.proposed_duration: 3 months of structured conservative management, with reassessment every 6 weeks
preconditions_for_failure: Worsening of myelopathic signs: decline in mJOA score by 2 or more points, new bowel or bladder dysfunction, or new motor weakness
Progression of gait impairment or falls
New or worsening cervical cord signal change on follow-up MRI
Intractable neuropathic pain unresponsive to conservative measures
Failure to show stabilization or improvement by 3 months
physiatrist_opening.public_message: While severe cervical stenosis with cord signal change and progressive myelopathy is concerning, I propose a time-limited trial of structured conservative management before surgery. The patient's deficits, though significant, have not shown acute deterioration, and surgery carries non-negligible risk given his poorly controlled hypertension and smoking history. A 3-month program of physical therapy, pain management, strict activity modification, and close monitoring is a reasonable first step. I estimate the conservative success rate in this specific presentation at approximately 10%—low but not zero—and therefore I cannot yet concede that surgery is the only option. The preconditions for declaring conservative failure are explicit: any worsening of myelopathic signs, new gait or balance decline, or intractable pain would trigger immediate surgical referral. Until those criteria are met, I maintain my stance for conservative care.

physiatrist_final.public_message: The Deputy Director asserts that this is a progressive cervical myelopathy with concordant imaging and that the priority is timely decompression, but this is not a new argument: I already weighed the progression and the cord signal change when I set my 10% success estimate and the strict failure criteria. No one has shown me a specific finding in the record that I have given too little weight, nor explained how waiting up to 3 months with close monitoring materially increases the risk of irreversible damage beyond what I have already accepted. The patient's deficits have been gradual, not acute, and his medical comorbidities make surgery far from risk-free. Therefore, I hold my recommendation for a time-limited conservative trial under the stated preconditions.

vice_opinions.assessment: This is a 63-year-old man with progressive cervical myelopathy (Nurick 3, mJOA 15), severe stenosis from C2-C3 to C5-C6, and cord signal change at C5-C6. The clinical and imaging findings are concordant, and without decompression he is at high risk of further, possibly irreversible, neurologic decline. Surgery is indicated; the main uncertainty is the optimal surgical approach given the long segment and unknown sagittal alignment.
proposed_options: Posterior cervical laminectomy C2-C6 with instrumented fusion C2-C6
Cervical laminoplasty C3-C6 with C2 dome laminectomy (if lordotic, no instability)
Anterior cervical corpectomy/discectomy with fusion (if kyphotic or ventral compression dominant)
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Posterior cervical laminectomy C2-C6 with instrumented fusion C2-C6
disagreement_points: I disagree with the physiatrist's proposal for a 3-month conservative trial: progressive myelopathy with cord signal change carries a real risk of irreversible neurologic worsening, and a 10% success estimate does not justify delaying decompression.
The extent of decompression must include C2-C3 if that level is contributing; a C3-C6-only procedure may leave residual stenosis and ongoing myelopathy.

We lack standing radiographs to assess sagittal alignment and dynamic instability; that should determine posterior versus anterior strategy, and the surgical plan should not be finalized without them.
deferred_questions_to_director: Should we proceed with surgical booking while optimizing blood pressure and smoking cessation, or require a formal optimization window first?
Would you prefer to obtain flexion/extension radiographs and a CT before selecting the approach, or is the MRI sufficient for posterior-only planning?
Do you want intraoperative neuromonitoring and a postoperative ICU bed arranged given ASA III and hypertension?
vice_opinions.public_message: From the surgical standpoint, this is a progressive cervical myelopathy with concordant imaging; the priority is timely decompression, not a trial of conservative care. I favor posterior decompression from C2 to C6 with instrumented fusion, though the final approach should be decided after we see standing films to confirm alignment. We can optimize his blood pressure and smoking in parallel with surgical preparation.

director_rulings.final_decision: Despite the physiatrist's request for a conservative trial, the progressive cervical myelopathy with severe stenosis C2-C6 and cord signal change warrants urgent surgical decompression. I am ruling for operative intervention: posterior cervical laminectomy C2-C6 with instrumented fusion, with preoperative standing flexion/extension radiographs and CT to confirm alignment and finalize approach; if significant kyphosis or instability is found, an anterior or combined approach will be considered. Blood pressure optimization and smoking cessation will proceed in parallel, and intraoperative neuromonitoring with a postoperative ICU bed are arranged.
director_rulings.surgical_plan: Posterior cervical laminectomy C2-C6 with instrumented fusion, to be performed after standing flexion/extension radiographs and CT confirm sagittal alignment; if significant kyphosis or dynamic instability is identified, anterior or combined approach will be considered.
delegated_tasks: Resident: book operating room time and arrange preoperative flexion/extension radiographs and CT cervical spine.
Anesthesiologist: perform airway assessment, arrange intraoperative neuromonitoring, and reserve a postoperative ICU bed.
Resident/primary team: optimize blood pressure and smoking cessation in parallel with surgical booking.

director_rulings.public_message: I have ruled for operative decompression without a conservative trial. The progressive myelopathy and cord signal change make surgery the indicated treatment. We will proceed with posterior cervical laminectomy C2-C6 and instrumented fusion after obtaining standing flexion/extension radiographs and a CT to confirm alignment; if significant kyphosis or instability is found, we will adjust the approach accordingly.
